strengths: Elegant general theoretical framework with distribution-free, finite-sample guarantees that apply to diverse inference problems (conformal prediction, hypothesis testing, risk control, multiple testing)
Novel 'black-box' interpretation treating base inference methods as modular components without modifying their inner workings, unlike prior work (SPI)
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple domains (protein structure prediction, LLM reasoning, outlier detection) with systematic ablation studies on key parameters
Mathematically rigorous treatment using partial order structures (Condition F.1) that unifies heterogeneous inference problems; includes impossibility results clarifying fundamental limits
Well-written presentation with pedagogical examples before general framework; comprehensive appendix with full proofs and detailed experimental specifications
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Core mechanism (three algorithm runs with min/max aggregation) is relatively straightforward; explicitly acknowledged as reformulation of SPI with main difference being 'black-box' treatment

Conservative general bounds: Theorem 3.2 depends on total variation distance d_{ℓ,Alg}(P,Q) which can be substantial; gap between general and problem-specific bounds (Section H) suggests framework may be loose for many applications

Lack of principled guidance for critical parameter ε: No principled selection rule, only informal guidance ('relative to α levels'); missing sensitivity analysis and no discussion of bias-variance tradeoff

Absent practical methods for synthetic data quality assessment: While claiming 'no assumptions on synthetic data,' success critically depends on quality (Figure 6d shows dramatic power loss); no tools to assess quality or select among multiple sources

Small sample sizes limit practical confidence: Experiments use n=10 (protein), n=15 (LLM), n=40-100 (outliers); unclear if modest improvements (Figure 3-5) scale to realistic settings with larger real sample sizes

Modest empirical improvements with unclear practical significance: GESPI achieves ~7% risk vs OnlyReal's 0% (but 100% abstention); power improvements often within error bars; Oracle gap remains substantial
Unfair baseline comparisons: OnlySynth lacks error guarantees making comparisons non-informative; no comparison with semi-supervised learning or domain adaptation methods
Computational cost not addressed: Running base algorithm three times has implications, especially for expensive methods; no computational trade-off analysis
Two-sided guardrails under-developed: Primary version (one-sided) used in experiments; two-sided theory relegated to appendix with less integration
Missing practical guidance: No principled ε selection, methods to detect poor synthetic data quality, or guidance on when GESPI outperforms standard approaches

strengths: Genuine theoretical contribution: distribution-free, finite-sample guarantees without assumptions on synthetic data distribution (Theorems 3.2-3.3) are non-trivial and broadly applicable

Elegant and practical 'wrapper' design: treats base methods as black boxes without modification, enabling seamless integration with conformal prediction, risk control, hypothesis testing, and multiple testing
Comprehensive theoretical development including impossibility results (Prop. E.1), application-specific bounds (Section H), and formal framework (Condition F.1) unifying multiple inference problems

Well-executed diverse experiments demonstrating practical utility on real applications (protein folding, LLM evaluation, outlier detection, Vision Transformer interpretability) with systematic ablations varying synthetic quality and ε
Adaptive behavior proven empirically: GESPI preserves error control at α+ε while approaching α when synthetic data aligns with real distribution
Reproducibility: detailed experimental protocols, full proofs, complete problem formulations enable verification and reproduction of results
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty relative to SPI (Bashari et al. 2025a): core construction (min/AND of outputs at α and α+ε) is conceptually straightforward; relationship to SPI not deeply analyzed; 'new interpretation' claim inadequately justified

Critical practical limitation: no principled method for selecting ε provided; experiments use ε=5% or 2% arbitrarily; sensitivity analysis (Figs 7,10) shows significant performance dependence on ε without guidance for practitioners

Misleading 'distribution-free' framing: when synthetic data is poor, method only guarantees α+ε error; all practical benefits require synthetic data similarity to real data, creating fundamental tension between theory's promises and practical utility

Opaque synthetic data quality assessment: bound in Theorem 3.2 depends on d_ℓ,Alg(P,Q)=d_TV(P_ℓ,Alg(P,Q), P_ℓ,Alg(Q,Q)) which is difficult to estimate in practice; no diagnostic methods provided to determine if synthetic data actually helps

Experiments use artificially small sample sizes (n=10 for protein prediction from 38 proteins, n=15-30 for AIME25) raising questions about real-world relevance; results at n=10 may not reflect practical utility at moderate sample sizes

Incomplete power analysis: no theoretical characterization of when/why synthetic data helps; no sample complexity results; Figure 5 shows GESPI often close to OnlyReal in power; missing finite-sample power bounds
Weak experimental baselines: OnlySynth is strawman baseline; missing comparisons to prediction-powered inference variants, domain adaptation methods, and direct comparison to SPI on same tasks

Practical gap between theory and practice: theoretical bounds depend on TV distances of score/parameter distributions that are hard to estimate; no guidance on when bounds are small enough to matter; implementation requires solving unsolved quality assessment problem

strengths: Addresses important and timely problem of safely leveraging synthetic data in statistical inference with distribution-free guarantees
General framework applicable to diverse inference problems (conformal prediction, hypothesis testing, risk control, multiple testing) without modifying base algorithms

Rigorous theoretical contributions: Theorem 3.3 provides adaptive risk bounds depending on synthetic data quality via total variation distance; Theorem 3.4 ensures utility bounds; Proposition E.1 characterizes fundamental limitations

Comprehensive experiments across diverse applications (ImageNet, AlphaFold protein structure prediction, outlier detection, LLM comparison, Vision Transformer interpretability) with careful ablation studies
Practical benefits demonstrated beyond theory: variance reduction in empirical error rates, improved ROC curves, maintained error control even with poor synthetic data
Black-box approach elegant and practical; Condition F.1 is mild and satisfied across diverse problems
Clear intuition: framework adapts automatically to synthetic data quality, achieving near-α performance with good data and safely degrading to α+ε with poor data
weaknesses: Fundamental limitation: relaxing error guarantee from α to α+ε appears necessary (proven by Prop E.1) but creates practical friction; paper lacks principled guidance on choosing ε (experiments use ε ∈ {1%, 2%, 5%, 10%} ad-hoc) and provides no adaptive selection methods

Critical gap in practical applicability: Theorem 3.3's bound depends on d_ℓ,Alg(P,Q) which is not observable from data and depends on unknown true distribution P; paper provides no methods to estimate this quantity a priori, making it unclear whether synthetic data quality justifies using GESPI before running it

Core technical novelty is limited: aggregation strategy (min/max of algorithm outputs) is conceptually straightforward; proofs rely primarily on monotonicity and taking extrema; total variation bounds are loose and not interpretable

Experimental design concerns: (1) synthetic data quality often opaque or post-hoc assessed via OnlySynth performance; (2) no methods proposed to filter or quality-check synthetic data; (3) small real sample sizes (n=10-15) though they motivate the approach; (4) SPI comparison incomplete, relegated to appendix despite being most relevant baseline

Limited characterization of when GESPI provides value: in poor-quality scenarios GESPI often matches OnlyReal (e.g., Figure S1d); paper lacks decision rules for practitioners or guidance on expected gains given synthetic data characteristics
For one-sided hypothesis testing, claimed flexibility assumes monotone likelihood ratio property which only holds for certain exponential families, restricting applicability

Practical gaps: no discussion of computational cost (tripling algorithm evaluations), no comparison to simple weighted averaging approaches, no guidance on when practitioners should ignore synthetic data entirely
